questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which gas makes up the largest fraction of dry air?
questions.answer: Nitrogen

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why is atmospheric composition important to life?
questions.answer: It supplies gases needed for respiration, photosynthesis and other natural processes while maintaining conditions suitable for life.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Explain the main composition of the atmosphere and the importance of its major components.
questions.answer: Award 1 mark for nitrogen as major constituent, 1 for oxygen, 1 for minor gases, 1 for role of oxygen, and 1 for role of carbon dioxide/nitrogen or another valid component.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which atmospheric gas is directly used by green plants in photosynthesis?
questions.answer: Carbon dioxide

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Distinguish a major atmospheric constituent from a trace constituent.
questions.answer: Major constituents occur in much larger proportions, while trace constituents occur in relatively small amounts.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Relate atmospheric gases to two biological and one environmental process.
questions.answer: Award marks for correct gas-process links: oxygen/respiration, carbon dioxide/photosynthesis, nitrogen cycle or greenhouse role, with explanation up to 5 marks.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which term describes tiny solid or liquid particles suspended in air?
questions.answer: Particulate matter

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: State two possible sources of air pollutants.
questions.answer: Vehicle exhaust, industrial emissions, fuel combustion, dust and burning wastes are suitable examples.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Explain how common air pollutants can affect human health and the environment.
questions.answer: Award marks for identifying pollutants/sources and explaining respiratory, visibility, ecosystem or material effects up to 5 marks.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Incomplete combustion can increase emission of which harmful gas?
questions.answer: Carbon monoxide

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why can particulate matter be harmful when inhaled?
questions.answer: Fine particles can enter the respiratory system and irritate or damage airways and lungs.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Compare gaseous pollutants and particulate pollutants with sources and effects.
questions.answer: Award 1 mark each for distinction, suitable gaseous source/effect, particulate source/effect, and a valid control idea.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Acid rain forms when certain pollutant gases react in the atmosphere to produce what?
questions.answer: Acidic substances

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: State one environmental effect of acid rain.
questions.answer: It can acidify water/soil, damage vegetation or accelerate deterioration of susceptible buildings and monuments.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Explain the formation and effects of acid rain.
questions.answer: Award marks for pollutant gases, atmospheric conversion to acids, dissolution in precipitation, and two valid effects.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Reducing sulfur-containing fuel emissions would most directly help reduce which problem?
questions.answer: Acid rain

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: How can acid rain damage carbonate-containing building materials?
questions.answer: Acids can react with carbonate minerals, causing gradual chemical deterioration of the material.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Suggest and explain strategies that can reduce acid-rain formation.
questions.answer: Award marks for reducing precursor emissions, cleaner fuels, emission treatment and two explanations/links to reduced acid formation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which process warms Earth when certain atmospheric gases absorb and re-emit infrared radiation?
questions.answer: Greenhouse effect

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Differentiate the greenhouse effect from global warming.
questions.answer: The greenhouse effect is the heat-trapping atmospheric process; enhanced greenhouse effect can raise average global temperature, producing global warming.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Explain how greenhouse gases contribute to global warming and give possible impacts.
questions.answer: Award marks for greenhouse gases, infrared absorption/re-emission, enhanced heat retention, and two valid climate impacts.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which human activity can increase atmospheric carbon dioxide?
questions.answer: Burning fossil fuels

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why can deforestation contribute to increased atmospheric carbon dioxide?
questions.answer: It reduces carbon dioxide removal by photosynthesis and may release stored carbon when biomass is burned or decomposes.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Relate fossil-fuel use and deforestation to climate change and mitigation.
questions.answer: Award marks for CO2 emissions, reduced uptake, greenhouse effect, and two mitigation links.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: What is a main purpose of a catalytic converter in vehicle exhaust?
questions.answer: Reduce harmful exhaust pollutants

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: State two strategies for reducing air pollution.
questions.answer: Examples include cleaner fuels, catalytic converters, emission controls, renewable energy, efficient transport and tree planting.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Evaluate several practical strategies for reducing environmental pollution.
questions.answer: Award marks for four valid strategies plus one explanation of how a strategy reduces emissions or exposure.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Replacing some fossil-fuel electricity with renewable energy can directly reduce what?
questions.answer: Combustion-related emissions

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: How can tree planting contribute to environmental improvement?
questions.answer: Trees can remove carbon dioxide by photosynthesis, store carbon and provide ecological benefits when appropriately planted and maintained.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Explain how technology and behavior can work together to reduce environmental problems.
questions.answer: Award marks for technology controls, cleaner energy, transport/energy behavior, conservation/tree planting, and integration/explanation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A hydrocarbon contains which elements only?
questions.answer: Carbon and hydrogen

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Define a hydrocarbon.
questions.answer: A hydrocarbon is an organic compound composed only of carbon and hydrogen atoms.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Classify hydrocarbons using saturation and carbon bonding.
questions.answer: Award marks for hydrocarbon definition, saturated/unsaturated distinction, single vs multiple bonds, and suitable examples.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which class contains only carbon-carbon single bonds?
questions.answer: Saturated hydrocarbons

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: What is meant by a saturated hydrocarbon?
questions.answer: It contains only single carbon-carbon bonds and therefore has the maximum hydrogen content for its carbon skeleton.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Compare saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons.
questions.answer: Award marks for definitions, bond types, hydrogen content/reactivity distinction and examples.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: What is the general formula of open-chain alkanes?
questions.answer: CnH2n+2

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why are alkanes called saturated hydrocarbons?
questions.answer: Their carbon atoms are connected by single bonds and each carbon has its normal valency fully satisfied.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Explain the homologous series of alkanes.
questions.answer: Award marks for general formula, same functional class, successive CH2 difference, similar chemical properties and gradual physical-property change.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Successive members of an alkane homologous series differ by which unit?
questions.answer: CH2

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Write the molecular formula of the alkane with three carbon atoms.
questions.answer: Propane has molecular formula C3H8.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Relate molecular formula, structural formula and homologous-series position for simple alkanes.
questions.answer: Award marks for formula relation, carbon chain, hydrogen count and two correct examples/explanations.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The parent name of an alkane is primarily based on what?

options.text: Length of the longest carbon chain

questions.answer: Length of the longest carbon chain

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: What is the first step in naming a simple branched alkane?
questions.answer: Identify the longest continuous carbon chain to determine the parent alkane name.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Describe a systematic method for naming a simple branched alkane.
questions.answer: Award marks for longest chain, numbering, substituent identification, locants and correctly assembled name.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why is the longest carbon chain numbered from the nearer substituent end?

options.text: To give substituents the lowest possible locants

questions.answer: To give substituents the lowest possible locants

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: What information does a locant provide in an alkane name?
questions.answer: It indicates the carbon position at which a substituent is attached to the parent chain.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Explain how structural formulas support correct IUPAC naming of simple alkanes.
questions.answer: Award marks for identifying chain, branches, numbering, locants and consistency between structure and name.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Complete combustion of an alkane in excess oxygen mainly produces what?
questions.answer: Carbon dioxide and water

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: What type of reaction occurs when a hydrogen atom of an alkane is replaced by a halogen atom?
questions.answer: It is a substitution reaction.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Describe combustion and substitution as important reactions of alkanes.
questions.answer: Award marks for complete combustion reactants/products, energy release, substitution definition, halogen involvement and a valid equation/example description.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Hydrogenation is useful in hydrocarbon chemistry because it can do what?
questions.answer: Add hydrogen across unsaturation

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: What is meant by hydrogenation in hydrocarbon chemistry?
questions.answer: Hydrogenation is addition of hydrogen to an unsaturated carbon-carbon bond, typically using a catalyst, producing a more saturated compound.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Explain preparation/reaction pathways connecting unsaturated hydrocarbons and alkanes.
questions.answer: Award marks for hydrogen addition, catalyst/conditions concept, saturation change, product class and one appropriate reaction relationship.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which SI unit is used for amount of substance?
questions.answer: mole

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why are standard units important in chemistry?

options.text: They are only used in laboratories

questions.answer: They make measurements comparable

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: What is meant by an SI unit?
questions.answer: An SI unit is a standardized unit from the International System of Units used so measurements can be communicated and compared consistently.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why are prefixes such as milli- and micro- useful in chemical measurements?
questions.answer: They provide convenient ways to express very small or large quantities without repeatedly writing many zeros.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Explain why standardized units, prefixes and correct unit symbols are essential in chemistry.
questions.answer: Award 1 mark for standardization, 1 for comparison/reproducibility, 1 for correct unit symbols, 1 for prefixes handling scale, and 1 for a suitable chemical measurement example.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which practice best improves the reliability of repeated volume measurements?

options.text: Reading the scale at eye level

questions.answer: Reading the scale at eye level

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which action is most likely to reduce avoidable measurement error?

options.text: Mixing different unit systems without conversion
Recording fewer significant figures than observed

questions.answer: Using a suitable calibrated instrument

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: State two good practices when taking a liquid-volume reading.
questions.answer: Use an appropriate graduated instrument and read the meniscus at eye level, avoiding parallax.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why should the measuring instrument be chosen according to the required precision?
questions.answer: Different instruments have different scale divisions and uncertainties, so an instrument must be precise enough for the measurement purpose.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Describe five practical steps that can improve the quality of laboratory measurements.
questions.answer: Award 1 mark each for five valid practices such as choosing a suitable calibrated instrument, reading scales correctly, repeating measurements, recording units/significant digits carefully, and controlling experimental conditions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A set of measurements clustered closely together but far from the accepted value is best described as what?
questions.answer: Precise but not accurate

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A consistent offset in every measurement is most characteristic of which type of error?
questions.answer: Systematic error

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Differentiate between accuracy and precision.
questions.answer: Accuracy describes closeness to an accepted or true value; precision describes closeness of repeated measurements to one another.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Differentiate between systematic and random error.
questions.answer: Systematic error shifts measurements consistently in one direction, whereas random error causes unpredictable scatter among repeated measurements.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Explain accuracy, precision, systematic error and random error using one measurement example.
questions.answer: Award 1 mark for accuracy, 1 for precision, 1 for systematic error, 1 for random error, and 1 for a coherent example showing how these ideas affect repeated measurements.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: What should be done first before using an unfamiliar laboratory chemical?

options.text: Read its hazard information and instructions
Transfer it to an unlabelled container

questions.answer: Read its hazard information and instructions

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why must chemical containers remain clearly labelled?

options.text: To guarantee the chemical is harmless
To remove the need for PPE

questions.answer: To identify contents and hazards

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: What is meant by a chemical hazard?
questions.answer: A chemical hazard is a property or condition of a substance that can cause harm, such as toxicity, corrosiveness, flammability or reactivity.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why should chemicals never be returned to the stock bottle after use?
questions.answer: Returning unused chemical can contaminate the stock and create unpredictable reactions or inaccurate future results.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Describe five principles for safe handling and storage of laboratory chemicals.
questions.answer: Award 1 mark each for five valid principles such as reading labels/hazard information, correct storage, avoiding direct contact/inhalation, using suitable PPE, preventing contamination, and following disposal instructions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: What is the main purpose of a hazard symbol on a chemical label?

options.text: To show the chemical is safe to taste
To communicate a specific risk quickly
To indicate the price of the chemical

questions.answer: To communicate a specific risk quickly

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A flammable warning indicates that the material should be kept away from what?
questions.answer: Ignition sources

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why are standardized hazard signs useful in laboratories?
questions.answer: They provide rapid, widely recognized visual warnings about specific dangers and help users choose appropriate precautions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: What should a student do after noticing a hazard sign on a reagent bottle?
questions.answer: Identify the indicated hazard, read the instructions, and apply the required handling, PPE and storage precautions before use.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Explain how hazard signs support risk assessment before an experiment begins.
questions.answer: Award 1 mark for identifying the hazard class, 1 for selecting PPE, 1 for handling precautions, 1 for storage/segregation implications, and 1 for emergency or disposal planning.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which item is designed primarily to protect the eyes in a chemistry laboratory?
questions.answer: Safety goggles

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why is a laboratory coat useful during practical work?

options.text: It removes the need to wash hands
It provides a protective barrier for clothing and skin

questions.answer: It provides a protective barrier for clothing and skin

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Name two common items of PPE and state what they protect.
questions.answer: Safety goggles protect the eyes, while a laboratory coat helps protect skin and clothing; suitable gloves may protect hands when required.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why must PPE be selected according to the specific experiment rather than worn randomly?
questions.answer: Different hazards require different protection, so PPE should match the risks identified for the chemicals and procedures being used.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Explain the role, selection and limitations of personal protective equipment in a chemistry laboratory.
questions.answer: Award 1 mark for eye protection, 1 for body/hand protection, 1 for matching PPE to risk, 1 for correct use/condition, and 1 for recognizing that PPE complements rather than replaces safe procedures.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why should students know the location of safety equipment before practical work begins?

options.text: So it can be reached quickly in an emergency
So it can be moved randomly

questions.answer: So it can be reached quickly in an emergency

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which principle is most important when using emergency safety equipment?

options.text: Use the correct equipment for the type of emergency

questions.answer: Use the correct equipment for the type of emergency

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why must access routes to emergency equipment remain clear?
questions.answer: Blocked access wastes critical time during an emergency and can prevent the correct safety equipment from being used promptly.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: What should students learn about safety equipment besides its location?
questions.answer: They should know its purpose, basic operating procedure, limitations, and when to alert the teacher or emergency personnel.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Describe how a laboratory should prepare students to use safety equipment effectively.
questions.answer: Award 1 mark for locating equipment, 1 for keeping access clear, 1 for explaining correct purpose/use, 1 for drills or demonstrations, and 1 for reporting/escalation procedures.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: If a laboratory accident occurs, what is the best immediate general response?

options.text: Alert the responsible teacher and follow the emergency procedure

questions.answer: Alert the responsible teacher and follow the emergency procedure

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why are emergency drills useful in a laboratory?

options.text: They are only for record keeping
They help people respond quickly and correctly

questions.answer: They help people respond quickly and correctly

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why should laboratory accidents be reported immediately?
questions.answer: Immediate reporting allows hazards to be controlled quickly, appropriate first aid or emergency action to begin, and further harm to be prevented.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: What is the purpose of an emergency drill?
questions.answer: An emergency drill rehearses roles, routes and actions so people can respond more quickly and safely during a real incident.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Outline a general five-step response to a laboratory emergency without assuming a specific accident type.
questions.answer: Award 1 mark each for stopping work/avoiding further exposure, alerting the responsible adult, identifying the hazard, using the correct emergency procedure/equipment only when appropriate, and documenting/reporting the incident after safety is restored.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: Which science studies the composition, properties and transformations of matter?
questions.answer: Chemistry

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: Which situation is most directly a chemistry question?

options.text: Why a planet follows an orbit
Why a lens forms an image
Why a substance changes into a different substance during a reaction

questions.answer: Why a substance changes into a different substance during a reaction

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: State what chemistry studies and name two kinds of information chemists seek about matter.
questions.answer: Chemistry studies matter and its changes. Chemists investigate properties, composition, structure and transformations; any two are sufficient.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: A metal sample changes colour after reacting with air. Explain why this observation belongs to chemistry.
questions.answer: It involves the properties of matter and a chemical transformation that produces material with different composition or properties.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: Why is energy often considered when studying chemical change?
questions.answer: Chemical changes involve rearrangement of particles and bonds, so energy can be absorbed, released or transferred during the change.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: Explain how chemistry connects the study of matter with observable changes. Include composition, properties and energy in your answer.
questions.answer: A complete answer should explain that chemistry examines what substances are made of, how their properties arise, how substances transform, and how energy may be absorbed or released during those transformations.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: Which state of matter usually has a fixed shape and a fixed volume?
questions.answer: Solid

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: Why can a gas be compressed much more easily than a solid?

options.text: Solids contain no empty space at all
Gas particles are much farther apart
Solid particles are always moving faster

questions.answer: Gas particles are much farther apart

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: Compare the arrangement of particles in a solid and a gas.
questions.answer: Solid particles are closely packed and remain near fixed positions, while gas particles are far apart and move freely through the available space.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: Explain why liquids can flow but are not compressed easily.
questions.answer: Liquid particles are close together, so there is little empty space for compression, but they can move past one another, allowing flow.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: What is plasma, and how does it differ from an ordinary gas?
questions.answer: Plasma is an ionized state containing charged particles such as ions and electrons. An ordinary gas is largely made of neutral particles.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: Compare solids, liquids, gases and plasma in terms of particle spacing, movement, shape, volume and compressibility.
questions.answer: A strong answer should compare each state: solids have closely packed particles, fixed shape and volume, and low compressibility; liquids have close particles, fixed volume but variable shape, and can flow; gases have widely spaced particles, variable shape and volume, and high compressibility; plasma is an energetic ionized state containing charged particles.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: Which description best defines an element?

options.text: A substance that always contains ions
Any material that can be separated by filtration
A pure substance made of one kind of atom

questions.answer: A pure substance made of one kind of atom

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: Which classification is used for elements according to general chemical and physical character?

options.text: Acids, bases, salts and oxides only
Metals, non-metals, metalloids and noble gases

questions.answer: Metals, non-metals, metalloids and noble gases

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: Define an element and explain why it is considered a pure substance.
questions.answer: An element is made of one kind of atom. It is a pure substance because its particles have a single chemical identity and it cannot be separated into simpler substances by ordinary chemical means.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: Can two different elements be in the same physical state? Explain with an example.
questions.answer: Yes. Physical state does not define chemical identity. For example, many different elements are solids at room temperature while still having different atomic identities.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: Name the four broad classes of elements highlighted in this chapter and state one feature used to distinguish them.
questions.answer: Metals, non-metals, metalloids and noble gases. They are distinguished using patterns in physical and chemical properties such as conductivity, reactivity or metallic character.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: Explain the idea of an element and describe how elements can be grouped by broad physical and chemical character.
questions.answer: A complete answer should define an element as a pure substance of one kind of atom, note that an element has its own chemical identity, and describe the broad groups metals, non-metals, metalloids and noble gases using general property differences.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: What is the term for different structural forms of the same element?
questions.answer: Allotropy

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: Which pair represents different structural forms of the same element?
questions.answer: Diamond and graphite

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: Define allotropy and give one example of an element that shows it.
questions.answer: Allotropy is the existence of an element in two or more different structural forms. Carbon is an example because it can occur as diamond, graphite and fullerene.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: Why can allotropes of the same element have different physical properties?
questions.answer: Their atoms are arranged or bonded differently, which changes structure and therefore properties even though the chemical element is the same.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: Give one structural difference between diamond and graphite.
questions.answer: Diamond has a three-dimensional giant covalent network, whereas graphite consists of layered sheets of carbon atoms.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: Explain how structural arrangement can produce different allotropes of one element. Use carbon as an example.
questions.answer: A complete answer should state that allotropes contain the same element but differ in atomic arrangement or bonding. Carbon can form a three-dimensional network in diamond, layered sheets in graphite, and cage-like fullerene structures, leading to different properties.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: Which sample is formed when substances are physically combined without a fixed chemical ratio?
questions.answer: A mixture

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: Which statement best distinguishes a compound from a mixture?

options.text: A compound can always be separated by filtration
A mixture always contains only two substances
A mixture has a fixed chemical formula
A compound has constituents chemically combined in a fixed ratio

questions.answer: A compound has constituents chemically combined in a fixed ratio

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: State one difference between an element and a compound.
questions.answer: An element contains one kind of atom and cannot be chemically decomposed into simpler substances, while a compound contains two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: Why can the components of a mixture often be separated by physical methods?
questions.answer: The components are not chemically bonded into a new substance, so differences in physical properties can be used to separate them.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: Compare the composition of a compound with the composition of a mixture.
questions.answer: A compound has a fixed composition determined by a definite ratio of elements, whereas a mixture can have variable composition.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: Compare elements, compounds and mixtures in terms of composition, particle identity, separation and purity.
questions.answer: A complete answer should explain that an element is a pure substance of one kind of atom; a compound is a pure substance of elements chemically combined in fixed ratios and separated only by chemical means; and a mixture contains physically combined substances in variable proportions that can often be separated physically.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: Which type of mixture has particles that settle on standing and can be removed by ordinary filtration?
questions.answer: Suspension

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: Why do particles of a true solution pass through ordinary filter paper?

options.text: They settle before reaching the filter
They are dispersed at a very small particle scale
They are always heavier than the solvent
They are chemically converted into the filter paper

questions.answer: They are dispersed at a very small particle scale

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: Differentiate between a true solution and a suspension using particle visibility and settling.
questions.answer: In a true solution the dissolved particles are not visible and do not settle, while in a suspension larger particles may be visible and settle on standing.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: Why is filtration effective for many suspensions but not for true solutions?
questions.answer: Suspension particles are large enough to be trapped by filter pores, while dissolved particles in a true solution are small enough to pass through.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: How does a colloidal solution differ from both a true solution and a suspension?
questions.answer: Colloidal particles are larger than particles in a true solution but smaller than typical suspension particles. They generally do not settle on standing and are not easily removed by ordinary filtration.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter_name: States of Matter and Phase Changes
questions.question_text: Compare true solutions, colloidal solutions and suspensions in terms of particle size behaviour, visibility, settling and filtration.
questions.answer: A complete answer should state that true solutions have very small dispersed particles that are not visible, do not settle and pass through ordinary filter paper; colloids have intermediate-sized particles that generally remain dispersed; and suspensions have larger particles that may be visible, settle on standing and can often be filtered.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which subatomic particle carries a negative charge?
questions.answer: Electron

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: In the Bohr model, an electron farther from the nucleus generally has what kind of energy?

options.text: The same energy in every shell

questions.answer: Higher energy

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: State the relative charges of an electron, proton and neutron.
questions.answer: Electron: -1, proton: +1, neutron: 0.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why is the nucleus responsible for almost all of an atom’s mass?
questions.answer: Protons and neutrons are located in the nucleus and each has far greater mass than an electron, so almost all atomic mass is concentrated there.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: What is meant by an electron shell or energy level?
questions.answer: It is a permitted region/energy level around the nucleus associated with electrons of a particular range of energy.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Describe the main features of an atom using the nucleus, protons, neutrons, electrons and electron shells.
questions.answer: A complete answer should identify the small dense nucleus containing protons and neutrons, electrons outside the nucleus in energy levels/shells, the relative charges of the particles, and the concentration of most atomic mass in the nucleus.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: What does the atomic number of an element equal?

options.text: The number of protons in its nucleus
The total number of protons and neutrons

questions.answer: The number of protons in its nucleus

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: An atom has mass number 31 and atomic number 15. How many neutrons does it contain?

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Differentiate between atomic number and mass number.
questions.answer: Atomic number is the number of protons. Mass number is the total number of protons plus neutrons.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why does changing the number of protons change the identity of an element?
questions.answer: The proton number is the atomic number, and each element has a unique atomic number. Changing it produces a different element.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: An atom has atomic number 17 and mass number 37. Calculate its numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons if it is neutral.
questions.answer: Protons = 17; neutrons = 37 - 17 = 20; electrons = 17.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Explain how atomic number and mass number are used to describe an atom, and show how the number of neutrons is found from them.
questions.answer: A complete answer should define atomic number Z as proton count, mass number A as proton plus neutron count, note that neutral atoms have electrons equal to protons, and use N = A - Z to obtain neutrons.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Isotopes of the same element have the same number of which particle?
questions.answer: Protons

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Two neutral atoms have the same atomic number but different mass numbers. What are they?
questions.answer: Isotopes of the same element

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Define isotopes.
questions.answer: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same proton number but different numbers of neutrons and therefore different mass numbers.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why do isotopes of one element usually have very similar chemical properties?
questions.answer: They have the same proton number and, for neutral atoms, the same electron arrangement, which mainly determines chemical behaviour.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Distinguish between forming an ion and forming a different isotope of the same element.
questions.answer: Ion formation changes the number of electrons, while a different isotope has a different number of neutrons without changing the proton number.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Explain how isotopes can differ in mass while remaining the same element. Include proton number, neutron number and chemical identity.
questions.answer: A complete answer should explain that isotopes share the same proton number/atomic number, so they are the same element, but contain different neutron numbers, giving different mass numbers while leaving their basic chemical identity largely unchanged.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why is the relative atomic mass of many elements not a whole number?

options.text: It is a weighted average of naturally occurring isotopes
Every atom contains half a proton

questions.answer: It is a weighted average of naturally occurring isotopes

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: An element has 75% isotope X-10 and 25% isotope X-12. What is its relative atomic mass?

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: What is meant by relative atomic mass?
questions.answer: It is the weighted average mass of the atoms of an element relative to one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why must isotopic abundance be considered when calculating relative atomic mass?
questions.answer: Different isotopes occur in different proportions, so each isotope must contribute to the average according to its abundance.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: An element consists of 60% atoms of mass 20 and 40% atoms of mass 22. Calculate its relative atomic mass.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Describe how relative atomic mass is calculated from isotopic masses and percentage abundances.
questions.answer: A complete answer should explain that each isotopic mass is multiplied by its fractional or percentage abundance, the contributions are added, and the result is the weighted average relative to the carbon-12 reference.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which reason best explains why two atoms may form a chemical bond?

options.text: Bonding removes every electron from both atoms.
Bonding always adds an electron to each nucleus.
The bonded arrangement can have lower energy than the separate atoms.
All atoms must become positively charged.

questions.answer: The bonded arrangement can have lower energy than the separate atoms.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Explain how a more stable electron arrangement can favour chemical bonding.
questions.answer: When atoms bond they can reach a lower-energy, more stable arrangement of electrons; the bonding interaction is favourable when its formation lowers the overall energy.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why are atoms with complete outer electron shells often less reactive than atoms with incomplete shells?
questions.answer: A filled valence shell is relatively stable; such atoms have less tendency to gain, lose or share electrons to reach a stable configuration.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which interaction is the clearest example of ionic bond formation?

options.text: Two neutral molecules attract through temporary dipoles.
Two nonmetal atoms share one electron pair.
A metal atom releases free electrons into a solid lattice.
An electron is transferred from one atom to another, producing oppositely charged ions.

questions.answer: An electron is transferred from one atom to another, producing oppositely charged ions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Compare the electron movement in the formation of sodium chloride and a hydrogen molecule.
questions.answer: Sodium chloride forms by electron transfer to produce Na+ and Cl- ions held by electrostatic attraction; H2 forms when two H atoms share an electron pair.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Explain ionic and coordinate covalent bond formation using electron transfer and electron-pair donation.
questions.answer: Ionic bond: one atom transfers electron(s) to another, giving oppositely charged ions whose electrostatic attraction holds them together (2 marks). Coordinate covalent bond: a shared pair is supplied initially by one donor atom to an electron-pair acceptor (2 marks). Explain that the coordinate bond behaves as a covalent bond once formed (1 mark).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: What directly allows a piece of metal to conduct electricity when it is still solid?

options.text: Delocalised electrons can move through its lattice.
Each metal atom first becomes a gas.
Positive metal ions move out of the solid.
Electrons are completely trapped in isolated pairs.

questions.answer: Delocalised electrons can move through its lattice.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Use metallic bonding to explain why copper conducts electrical current without melting.
questions.answer: Mobile, delocalised electrons carry charge through the fixed lattice of positive metal ions while the solid metal structure remains intact.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Relate metallic bonding to electrical conduction and the ability of metals to be shaped.
questions.answer: Metallic bonding consists of positive metal ions attracted to delocalised electrons (2 marks). The mobile electrons carry charge through the solid (1 mark). Layers of ions can shift while the electron cloud continues to provide bonding, allowing malleability/ductility (2 marks).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A metal atom that loses its outer electron readily is described as having which tendency?

options.text: Strong electron-pair acceptance without ion formation
Negative ionic charge after losing an electron

questions.answer: Electropositive character

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Describe how a sodium atom becomes a positive ion and connect this to its electropositive character.
questions.answer: Sodium loses one outer-shell electron to form Na+. A tendency to lose electrons and form cations is characteristic of an electropositive element.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: How does the low energy needed to remove an outer electron generally affect a metal’s electropositive character?
questions.answer: A relatively small ionisation energy makes electron loss easier; this is consistent with stronger electropositive behaviour.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: When hydrogen and chlorine share electrons, why is their bond polar?

options.text: The shared electrons stop moving completely.
Both atoms have exactly the same attraction for the shared pair.
Chlorine attracts the shared pair more strongly than hydrogen.
Hydrogen transfers both of its electrons to chlorine.

questions.answer: Chlorine attracts the shared pair more strongly than hydrogen.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Define electronegativity in the context of a covalent bond.
questions.answer: Electronegativity is the tendency of a bonded atom to attract the shared electrons towards itself.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Describe the partial charges expected on H and Cl in a hydrogen chloride molecule.
questions.answer: Chlorine attracts the bonding electrons more strongly and develops a partial negative charge (δ−); hydrogen develops a partial positive charge (δ+).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which sample is expected to conduct electricity because its ions are free to move?
questions.answer: Molten sodium chloride

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why can a molten ionic compound conduct electricity while the same compound may not conduct as a rigid solid?
questions.answer: In the solid the ions occupy fixed lattice positions; on melting they can move and transport electric charge.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Compare a typical ionic compound and a simple molecular covalent compound in bonding, melting behaviour and electrical conduction.
questions.answer: Ionic compound: electrostatic attraction among cations/anions (1), usually higher melting point due to strong lattice forces (1), molten or dissolved state can conduct through mobile ions (1). Simple molecular covalent compound: atoms share electrons (1); it usually has weaker intermolecular attractions and is a poor electrical conductor because it lacks mobile charged particles (1).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which interaction is most directly responsible for the unusually strong attraction between nearby water molecules?

options.text: Transfer of electrons from one water molecule to another
Formation of an ionic lattice of water molecules

questions.answer: Hydrogen bonding

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Distinguish the covalent O–H bond within a water molecule from hydrogen bonding between water molecules.
questions.answer: The O–H bond is an intramolecular covalent bond formed by sharing electrons; a hydrogen bond is an intermolecular attraction between suitable polar molecules.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Explain why water can have a higher boiling point than a similar small molecular hydride that cannot form strong hydrogen bonds.
questions.answer: Water has polar O–H bonds (1) and forms a network of intermolecular hydrogen bonds (2). More energy is needed to overcome these attractions when liquid water vaporises (1), raising its boiling point relative to a comparable hydride with weaker attractions (1).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why can graphite conduct electricity along its layers?

options.text: All covalent bonds disappear in graphite.
Some electrons are mobile within the layered carbon structure.
Graphite is made of molten ionic crystals.
Every carbon atom becomes a free positive ion.

questions.answer: Some electrons are mobile within the layered carbon structure.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Explain how the bonding arrangement of graphite differs from that of diamond in a way that affects conductivity.
questions.answer: Graphite has layers containing electrons that can move within the sheets, allowing conduction; diamond forms a three-dimensional covalent network in which bonding electrons are localised, so diamond does not normally conduct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Explain why an ionic crystal is often brittle when stress shifts its layers.
questions.answer: A shift can bring ions of the same charge opposite one another; strong repulsion then causes the lattice to fracture instead of deforming plastically.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: How many atoms are represented by a single formula unit of Na2CO3?

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Interpret the subscripts in the formula Ca(OH)2.
questions.answer: The formula unit has one Ca, two O and two H atoms; the subscript 2 applies to both O and H inside the parentheses.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Determine the total number of atoms represented by the formula Al2(SO4)3.
questions.answer: 2 Al + 3 S + (4 × 3) O = 17 atoms per formula unit.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: What is the empirical formula of a compound with molecular formula C6H12O6?
questions.answer: CH2O

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Distinguish an empirical formula from a molecular formula.
questions.answer: An empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of constituent atoms, while a molecular formula gives the actual number of each type of atom in one molecule.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Reduce the molecular formula C4H10 to its empirical formula.
questions.answer: Divide both subscripts by 2: C2H5.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which formula gives an electrically neutral compound from Mg2+ and F− ions?
questions.answer: MgF2

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Explain why calcium nitride is represented by Ca3N2 rather than CaN.
questions.answer: Ca forms Ca2+ and nitrogen forms N3−; three Ca2+ ions (+6) balance two N3− ions (−6), giving Ca3N2.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Show how ionic charges determine the formulas of magnesium oxide and aluminium chloride.
questions.answer: For magnesium oxide identify Mg2+ and O2− (1 mark), balance 1:1 to write MgO (1). For aluminium chloride identify Al3+ and Cl− (1), balance 1:3 to write AlCl3 (1). Explain that each formula is electrically neutral (1).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A molecular compound has empirical formula CH and molecular molar mass six times its empirical-formula mass. What is its molecular formula?
questions.answer: C6H6

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Write the relationship between empirical-formula mass, molecular molar mass and molecular formula.
questions.answer: n = molecular molar mass ÷ empirical-formula mass (a positive whole number); molecular formula = n × empirical-formula subscripts.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A compound has empirical formula CH2O and molecular molar mass 180 g mol−1. Calculate its molecular formula.
questions.answer: Empirical-formula mass = 12 + 2(1) + 16 = 30 g mol−1 (2 marks). n = 180/30 = 6 (1). Multiply CH2O subscripts by six to obtain C6H12O6 (2).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: What molecular formula follows from the displayed structural sequence CH3–CH2–OH?
questions.answer: C2H6O

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Explain how you obtain the molecular formula from a structural formula.
questions.answer: Count each element symbol and all atoms of that element represented in the structural drawing, then write the totals as subscripts after the appropriate element symbols.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which quantity approximately corresponds to one mole of separate particles?
questions.answer: 6.02 × 10^23 particles

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: What is the purpose of Avogadro’s constant in chemistry?
questions.answer: It links amount of substance in moles to the number of specified entities: N = n × NA, where NA is approximately 6.02 × 10^23 mol−1.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Calculate the number of molecules in 0.50 mol of a pure molecular substance, using 6.02 × 10^23 mol−1.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: What is the approximate molar mass of CO2 if C = 12 and O = 16?
questions.answer: 44 g mol−1

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: State the equation linking mass, molar mass and amount of substance, and give the SI-related units normally used in school calculations.
questions.answer: n = m/M, with n in mol, mass m in grams and molar mass M in g mol−1.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: How many moles of CO2 are present in 22.0 g? Use M(CO2) = 44.0 g mol−1.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which is the balanced equation for hydrogen combining with oxygen to form water?

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why must a correctly balanced chemical equation have the same number of atoms of each element on its two sides?
questions.answer: Chemical reactions rearrange atoms rather than creating or destroying them, so the number of atoms of each element must be conserved.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Balance Fe + O2 → Fe2O3 and explain the physical meaning of the coefficients.
questions.answer: Balanced equation: 4Fe + 3O2 → 2Fe2O3 (2 marks). Explain that the coefficients express relative particle or mole counts 4:3:2 (1). Check Fe: 4 on each side and O: 6 on each side (2).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: For 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O, how many moles of water can form from 3 moles of O2 when hydrogen is in excess?
questions.answer: 6 mol

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Outline the main steps for converting a given reactant mass into a predicted product mass using a balanced equation.
questions.answer: Convert given mass to moles using molar mass; use the balanced coefficient ratio to find moles of product; convert product moles to mass using its molar mass.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: In 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O, what mass of water forms when 4.0 g of H2 reacts completely with excess O2? Use H2 = 2.0 g mol−1 and H2O = 18.0 g mol−1.
questions.answer: Moles H2 = 4.0/2.0 = 2.0 mol. The 2:2 ratio gives 2.0 mol H2O. Product mass = 2.0 × 18.0 = 36.0 g.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: For N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3, determine the number of moles of NH3 expected from 1.5 mol N2 with excess H2 and explain your ratio.
questions.answer: Read the balanced 1:2 mole ratio between N2 and NH3 (2 marks). Calculate 1.5 × 2 = 3.0 mol NH3 (2). Mention that H2 is in excess so nitrogen is the limiting reactant (1).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A sealed reaction vessel is the chosen system. Which item is part of its surroundings?

options.text: The reaction mixture inside the vessel
The reaction products inside the vessel
The laboratory air outside the vessel

questions.answer: The laboratory air outside the vessel.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: When a chemical system gives heat to its surroundings, in which direction has heat moved?

options.text: No energy can cross the boundary

questions.answer: Out of the system.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Define a system and its surroundings in a chemical experiment.
questions.answer: The system is the particular matter or reaction selected for study; the surroundings are everything outside that selected system.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: For warm water in a beaker selected as the system, identify the system and one possible surrounding.
questions.answer: The water is the system. The beaker material and the surrounding room air are examples of the surroundings.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Describe how you would identify a system, surroundings and heat transfer while measuring a reaction temperature change.
questions.answer: Identify the reaction mixture as the system (1 mark), the vessel and external air as surroundings (1), specify the system boundary (1), explain that energy may cross the boundary as heat (1), and relate the observed temperature change to heat entering or leaving the selected system with suitable experimental caution (1).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A reaction has products with lower enthalpy than its reactants. What is the sign of ΔH?

options.text: Impossible to determine because no product masses are stated

questions.answer: Negative

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which expression correctly represents enthalpy change at constant pressure for a reaction?
questions.answer: H(products) − H(reactants)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: State the sign convention for enthalpy change in exothermic and endothermic reactions.
questions.answer: An exothermic reaction releases heat and usually has ΔH < 0. An endothermic reaction absorbs heat and usually has ΔH > 0.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why is the enthalpy change of a reaction more useful experimentally than an absolute enthalpy value?
questions.answer: The heat transferred under specified conditions can be measured, allowing a difference between final and initial enthalpy to be determined; absolute total enthalpy is not directly measurable in a simple experiment.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The enthalpy assigned to reactants for a reaction is 180 kJ and to products is 125 kJ. Find ΔH and interpret its sign.
questions.answer: Use ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants) (2 marks). Substitute 125 − 180 = −55 kJ for the reaction as written (2). The negative sign indicates heat release/exothermic change (1).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: What is the best description of an endothermic chemical reaction?

options.text: The system gives heat to its surroundings
The reaction cannot involve chemical bonds
The system always becomes a metal
The system absorbs heat from its surroundings

questions.answer: The system absorbs heat from its surroundings.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which change requires energy input to overcome existing chemical bonds?
questions.answer: Bond breaking

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why may the container feel warmer during an exothermic reaction?
questions.answer: Heat released by the reaction system is transferred to the container and surroundings, raising their temperature.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Explain why making bonds and breaking bonds affect the energy balance of a reaction differently.
questions.answer: Breaking chemical bonds requires an input of energy, whereas forming new bonds releases energy; the net difference determines the reaction enthalpy change.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Compare exothermic and endothermic energy profiles using the relative levels of reactants and products.
questions.answer: For an exothermic process product enthalpy is below reactant enthalpy (1) and ΔH is negative (1). For an endothermic process product enthalpy is above reactant enthalpy (1) and ΔH is positive (1). Both processes may require a positive activation-energy barrier to begin (1).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: What effect does a suitable catalyst typically have on a reaction pathway?

options.text: It changes all reactants into different elements
It lowers the activation-energy requirement without changing overall ΔH
It makes product enthalpy equal to zero

questions.answer: It lowers the activation-energy requirement without changing overall ΔH.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: What does activation energy describe?

options.text: The heat capacity of the products
The minimum collision energy needed to pass the reaction barrier
The number of molecules in one mole

questions.answer: The minimum collision energy needed to pass the reaction barrier.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why can an energetically favourable reaction still proceed slowly at room temperature?
questions.answer: Reacting particles still need to overcome an activation-energy barrier; too few collisions may have enough energy or suitable orientation under those conditions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Does a catalyst change the enthalpy difference between reactants and products? Explain briefly.
questions.answer: No. A catalyst changes the reaction pathway and lowers its activation barrier, but the initial and final enthalpy states, and hence ΔH, remain unchanged.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Explain how a catalyst changes the progress of a reaction on an energy-pathway diagram.
questions.answer: Describe the uncatalysed curve with an activation peak (1 mark). The catalysed pathway has a lower peak/activation energy (2). Both pathways begin at the same reactant energy and end at the same product energy (1), so their overall ΔH is unchanged (1).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which process normally releases more usable energy per glucose molecule in living cells?

options.text: Aerobic respiration, when oxygen is available

questions.answer: Aerobic respiration, when oxygen is available.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which condition especially favours anaerobic breakdown of glucose in a cell?

options.text: Insufficient oxygen for normal aerobic respiration

questions.answer: Insufficient oxygen for normal aerobic respiration

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Give one fundamental difference between aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
questions.answer: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and generally releases more usable energy from glucose; anaerobic respiration occurs without oxygen and yields less energy per glucose.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: How does cellular respiration connect a food molecule to a cell’s energy needs?
questions.answer: Cells break down energy-rich food molecules through enzyme-controlled reactions and transfer some of the released chemical energy into usable forms, especially ATP.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration in oxygen requirement, products and relative energy output.
questions.answer: Aerobic respiration requires oxygen (1), commonly gives CO2 and water on complete glucose oxidation (1), and gives relatively more usable energy (1). Anaerobic processes do not require oxygen (1) and generally yield less usable energy; products vary, such as lactate in muscle cells or ethanol and CO2 in yeast (1).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which change best represents a reversible process under suitable conditions?
questions.answer: Hydrating and dehydrating a salt

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A reaction is called reversible when it can proceed in which way under the same set of conditions?

options.text: In both forward and reverse directions

questions.answer: In both forward and reverse directions

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: State one key difference between reversible and irreversible chemical reactions.
questions.answer: A reversible reaction can proceed in both forward and reverse directions under suitable conditions, whereas an irreversible reaction proceeds essentially in one direction under those conditions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why can dehydration followed by rehydration of a suitable hydrated salt illustrate reversibility?
questions.answer: Because removal of water can convert the hydrated form to another form, and supplying water again can restore the hydrated form, showing that the change can proceed in opposite directions under suitable conditions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Compare reversible and irreversible reactions and explain how a closed reaction vessel can help demonstrate reversibility.
questions.answer: Award 1 mark for defining irreversible reaction, 1 for defining reversible reaction, 1 for noting forward and reverse directions, 1 for explaining that a closed vessel prevents loss of participating substances, and 1 for linking retained reactants/products with the possibility of the reverse process.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: At dynamic equilibrium, which statement about reaction rates is correct?

options.text: Forward rate is greater than reverse rate
Reverse rate is greater than forward rate
Forward and reverse rates are equal

questions.answer: Forward and reverse rates are equal

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why may a reaction mixture look unchanged at dynamic equilibrium?

options.text: Reactant and product concentrations remain macroscopically constant

questions.answer: Reactant and product concentrations remain macroscopically constant

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why is chemical equilibrium described as dynamic rather than static?
questions.answer: Because forward and reverse reactions continue simultaneously, but at equal rates, so no overall macroscopic change in composition is observed.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Does dynamic equilibrium require equal concentrations of reactants and products? Explain briefly.
questions.answer: No. Dynamic equilibrium requires equal forward and reverse reaction rates. Reactant and product concentrations remain constant with time, but they do not have to be numerically equal.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Describe how a reversible reaction approaches dynamic equilibrium after reactants are mixed in a closed container.
questions.answer: Award 1 mark for initially dominant forward reaction, 1 for formation and accumulation of products, 1 for growth of the reverse reaction rate, 1 for equality of forward and reverse rates at equilibrium, and 1 for explaining that concentrations then remain constant macroscopically while both reactions continue.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: If some product is removed from a reversible system at equilibrium, which response helps restore equilibrium?

options.text: The forward reaction is favoured to replace some product
The reverse reaction is permanently stopped

questions.answer: The forward reaction is favoured to replace some product

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: What is the main effect of adding a suitable catalyst to a reversible reaction that can attain equilibrium?

options.text: It changes the equilibrium composition in favour of products
It changes the equilibrium composition in favour of reactants
It helps equilibrium to be reached faster by increasing both reaction rates
It makes the reverse reaction impossible

questions.answer: It helps equilibrium to be reached faster by increasing both reaction rates

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: How can changing the concentration of one component disturb an equilibrium?
questions.answer: Changing a component concentration makes the forward and reverse rates temporarily unequal. The system then shifts through additional reaction until a new equilibrium with equal rates is established.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Distinguish the role of a catalyst from the role of temperature or pressure in an equilibrium system.
questions.answer: A catalyst mainly changes how quickly equilibrium is reached by accelerating both directions. Temperature or, for suitable gaseous systems, pressure can change the equilibrium position and therefore the equilibrium composition.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Explain how concentration, temperature, pressure and a catalyst can be used when managing a reversible reaction at equilibrium.
questions.answer: Award 1 mark for concentration change causing a shift that opposes the disturbance, 1 for temperature affecting the preferred direction according to heat effects, 1 for pressure affecting gaseous equilibria depending on gas amounts on each side, 1 for a catalyst speeding both directions and reducing time to equilibrium without changing equilibrium composition, and 1 for linking these controls to improved process yield or operating efficiency.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which substance is best classified as an alkali?
questions.answer: A water-soluble base

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which description best distinguishes many natural acids from mineral acids?

options.text: Natural acids are commonly obtained from biological sources
Mineral acids cannot dissolve in water

questions.answer: Natural acids are commonly obtained from biological sources

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Differentiate between a base and an alkali.
questions.answer: A base is a substance that shows basic behavior, while an alkali is specifically a base that is soluble in water.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Give one reason why sour-tasting food materials may show acidic behavior.
questions.answer: Many such food materials contain naturally occurring organic acids that can produce acidic properties in aqueous conditions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Compare acids, bases and alkalis using their general chemical character and solubility relationship.
questions.answer: Award 1 mark for identifying acidic behavior, 1 for identifying basic behavior, 1 for defining an alkali as a water-soluble base, 1 for giving a suitable acid example, and 1 for giving a suitable base/alkali example with correct classification.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: According to the Arrhenius concept, an acid increases the concentration of which ion in water?
questions.answer: H+

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which observation most directly supports calling NaOH an Arrhenius base?

options.text: It forms a precipitate in every reaction
It produces OH- ions in aqueous solution
It accepts electrons from a metal

questions.answer: It produces OH- ions in aqueous solution

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: State the Arrhenius definitions of an acid and a base.
questions.answer: An Arrhenius acid produces H+ ions in aqueous solution, while an Arrhenius base produces OH- ions in aqueous solution.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: What is the difference between a strong acid and a weak acid in terms of ionization?
questions.answer: A strong acid ionizes essentially completely in aqueous solution, whereas a weak acid ionizes only partially under comparable conditions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Explain the Arrhenius concept of acids and bases and include one limitation of this concept.
questions.answer: Award 1 mark for acid definition, 1 for base definition, 1 for emphasizing aqueous solution, 1 for a correct acid/base example, and 1 for noting that the concept is limited because it does not cover all acid-base behavior outside simple H+/OH- production in water.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A Bronsted-Lowry base is a species that does what?

options.text: Must contain OH- in its formula

questions.answer: Accepts a proton

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: When a Bronsted-Lowry acid donates a proton, the species left behind is its what?
questions.answer: Conjugate base

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Define Bronsted-Lowry acid and base.
questions.answer: A Bronsted-Lowry acid donates a proton, while a Bronsted-Lowry base accepts a proton.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why can water behave as both a Bronsted-Lowry acid and a Bronsted-Lowry base?
questions.answer: Water can donate a proton in one reaction and accept a proton in another, depending on the reacting partner, so it can display amphoteric acid-base behavior.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Explain proton transfer in a Bronsted-Lowry acid-base reaction and show how conjugate acid-base pairs arise.
questions.answer: Award 1 mark for identifying the acid as proton donor, 1 for base as proton acceptor, 1 for explaining proton transfer, 1 for identifying the conjugate base formed from the acid, and 1 for identifying the conjugate acid formed from the base.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which gas is commonly produced when a suitable acid reacts with an active metal?
questions.answer: Hydrogen

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A reaction between an acid and a suitable base is commonly described as what?
questions.answer: Neutralization

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: What products are generally formed when an acid reacts with a metal carbonate?
questions.answer: A salt, water and carbon dioxide are generally formed.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why is neutralization useful when excess acid must be reduced?
questions.answer: A suitable base reacts with the acid and reduces its acidic character, commonly producing a salt and water.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Describe three characteristic reactions of acids and two characteristic reactions of bases.
questions.answer: Award 1 mark each for three correct acid reaction types such as with active metals, bases/metal oxides, and carbonates/hydrogen carbonates, plus 1 mark for reaction of a base with an acid and 1 mark for another suitable base reaction such as with an ammonium salt.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Acid rain is most closely associated with atmospheric formation of which type of substances?
questions.answer: Acidic compounds from pollutant gases

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which environmental effect is consistent with prolonged acid rain exposure?

options.text: Damage to sensitive vegetation and materials
Permanent removal of all atmospheric gases
Conversion of every lake into distilled water

questions.answer: Damage to sensitive vegetation and materials

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: What is acid rain?
questions.answer: Acid rain is precipitation that becomes more acidic than normal because acidic substances form in the atmosphere from pollutant gases and dissolve in water droplets.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: State two possible harmful effects of acid rain.
questions.answer: It can damage vegetation and aquatic ecosystems, and it can also accelerate deterioration of buildings, monuments or other susceptible materials.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Explain how acid rain forms and discuss four consequences or control considerations.
questions.answer: Award 1 mark for linking pollutant gases with atmospheric acid formation, 1 for incorporation into precipitation, 1 for an effect on plants/ecosystems, 1 for an effect on buildings/materials or water bodies, and 1 for a sensible control principle such as reducing emissions of acid-forming pollutants.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: What determines the left-to-right order of elements in the modern periodic table?

options.text: Decreasing atomic mass in every case

questions.answer: Increasing atomic number

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: What is a vertical column in the periodic table called?
questions.answer: Group

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Distinguish between a period and a group in the modern periodic table.
questions.answer: A period is a horizontal row of elements, while a group is a vertical column of elements.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why do elements in the same group often have similar chemical properties?
questions.answer: They have similar outer-shell electronic configurations, especially similar numbers of valence electrons, which leads to similar chemical behavior.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Explain how atomic number, periods and groups organize the modern periodic table.
