questions.answer: Award 1 mark for increasing atomic-number order, 1 for defining periods, 1 for defining groups, 1 for linking periods to changing electron shells/configurations, and 1 for linking groups to similar valence-shell patterns and chemical properties.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: An element has three occupied electron shells. Which periodic-table feature is most directly indicated?
questions.answer: Its period number

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which information is most useful for locating an element in a group when its atomic number is known?
questions.answer: Its outer-shell electron arrangement

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: How can electronic configuration help identify the period of an element?
questions.answer: The number of occupied principal electron shells indicates the period in which the element is located.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: How can valence electrons help predict the group behavior of a main-group element?
questions.answer: Elements with similar numbers of valence electrons tend to fall in related groups and show similar bonding or ion-forming behavior.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Describe how electronic configuration can be used to predict an element’s period, group tendency and broad chemical behavior.
questions.answer: Award 1 mark for using occupied shells to identify period, 1 for using valence electrons to infer group tendency, 1 for linking valence electrons to ion formation, 1 for linking group placement to similar chemical properties, and 1 for a consistent example or explanation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A Group 1 element most commonly forms which ion?

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A Group 17 element commonly forms an ion with which charge?

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why do many Group 1 elements form 1+ ions?
questions.answer: They can lose one valence electron to reach a more stable outer-shell arrangement, leaving the atom with one more proton than electrons.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why do many Group 17 elements form 1- ions?
questions.answer: They tend to gain one electron to complete the outer shell, giving the ion one more electron than protons.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Explain how periodic-table group position can help predict common ionic charges for main-group elements.
questions.answer: Award 1 mark for linking group position to valence electrons, 1 for explaining electron loss by metals, 1 for explaining electron gain by non-metals, 1 for a correct Group 1 or 2 example, and 1 for a correct Group 16 or 17 example.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Across a period from left to right, atomic radius generally does what?
questions.answer: Decreases

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Across a period from left to right, electronegativity generally does what?
questions.answer: Increases

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why does atomic radius generally increase down a group?
questions.answer: Additional electron shells are added down the group and inner electrons shield the outer electrons from the nucleus, increasing atomic size.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why does first ionization energy generally increase across a period?
questions.answer: Effective nuclear attraction on the outer electrons generally increases while atomic radius decreases, so more energy is required to remove an electron.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Compare the general trends of atomic radius, ionization energy and electronegativity across a period and down a group.
questions.answer: Award 1 mark for radius decreasing across a period, 1 for radius increasing down a group, 1 for ionization energy generally increasing across and decreasing down, 1 for electronegativity generally increasing across and decreasing down, and 1 for explaining these trends using nuclear attraction, shells and shielding.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why does Group 1 reactivity generally increase down the group?

options.text: Valence electrons become more tightly held
The outer electron becomes easier to remove

questions.answer: The outer electron becomes easier to remove

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which broad description best fits Group 1 elements except hydrogen?
questions.answer: Alkali metals

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why are Group 1 metals generally very reactive?
questions.answer: They have one valence electron that can be removed relatively easily, allowing them to form stable positive ions and react readily.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: State one physical and one chemical trend down Group 1.
questions.answer: A suitable response is that melting point generally decreases while chemical reactivity generally increases down the group.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Explain the change in reactivity and selected physical properties of Group 1 elements down the group.
questions.answer: Award 1 mark for increasing atomic size, 1 for increased shielding/weaker attraction to the outer electron, 1 for easier electron loss, 1 for increased reactivity, and 1 for a correct physical trend such as decreasing melting point or changing density.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Group 17 elements are commonly called what?
questions.answer: Halogens

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: How does halogen reactivity generally change down Group 17?
questions.answer: Decreases

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why are Group 17 elements called halogens?
questions.answer: They readily form salts when they react with suitable metals, so the name reflects their salt-forming behavior.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why does the oxidizing strength of halogens generally decrease down the group?
questions.answer: Increasing atomic size and shielding reduce the attraction for an incoming electron, so the tendency to gain electrons generally decreases down the group.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Describe the general physical and chemical trends of Group 17 elements down the group.
questions.answer: Award 1 mark for increasing atomic size/density trend, 1 for change in physical state or boiling/melting tendencies, 1 for decreasing reactivity, 1 for decreasing oxidizing ability, and 1 for explaining the electron-gain trend using shielding and nuclear attraction.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which property is commonly associated with many transition elements?

options.text: Always being gases at room temperature
Extremely low density in every case

questions.answer: Useful catalytic activity

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Transition elements are best described broadly as what?
questions.answer: Metals with characteristic metallic properties

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: State two general physical properties often shown by transition metals.
questions.answer: They commonly have relatively high densities and high melting points, and they also show metallic strength and conductivity.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why are transition metals important in industrial catalysis?
questions.answer: Many transition metals or their compounds can provide effective catalytic surfaces or pathways that increase reaction rates without being consumed overall.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Summarize important physical and chemical features of transition elements and relate one feature to industrial use.
questions.answer: Award 1 mark for metallic character, 1 for high density, 1 for relatively high melting point/strength, 1 for catalytic behavior, and 1 for linking a catalyst property to a suitable industrial application.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why are noble gases generally unreactive?

options.text: Their outer electron shells are complete

questions.answer: Their outer electron shells are complete

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: How do noble gases normally exist under ordinary conditions?
questions.answer: As monatomic gases

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: What feature of noble-gas electronic structure explains their low reactivity?
questions.answer: Their outermost electron shells are complete, giving them a stable electronic arrangement and little tendency to gain or lose electrons.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why are noble gases described as monatomic?
questions.answer: Their atoms normally exist as separate individual atoms rather than being bonded into molecules under ordinary conditions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Explain the relationship between noble-gas electronic configuration, monatomic existence and chemical unreactivity.
questions.answer: Award 1 mark for complete outer shell, 1 for stable configuration, 1 for low tendency to gain electrons, 1 for low tendency to lose/share electrons, and 1 for relating this stability to monatomic, generally unreactive behavior.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which property is more typical of metals than non-metals?

options.text: Poor thermal conductivity in every case

questions.answer: Good electrical conductivity

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which statement best describes many non-metals?

options.text: They all form positive ions only
They are usually poor electrical conductors compared with metals
They are all shiny malleable solids

questions.answer: They are usually poor electrical conductors compared with metals

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: State two physical differences between metals and non-metals.
questions.answer: Metals are generally better conductors and are often malleable/ductile, while non-metals are generally poorer conductors and solid non-metals are often brittle.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Why is graphite treated as an important exception when comparing metals and non-metals?
questions.answer: Graphite is a non-metal form of carbon but can conduct electricity, showing that broad metal/non-metal trends have exceptions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Compare the general physical properties of metals and non-metals and mention one important exception.
questions.answer: Award 1 mark for conductivity comparison, 1 for malleability/ductility comparison, 1 for lustre or density/strength comparison, 1 for state/brittleness comparison, and 1 for a correct exception such as graphite conducting electricity.
